questions.prompt: After one update at state s with alpha = 0.2 and delta = 0.5, features are phi(s) = [1, 3] and phi(t) = [1, 1]. By how much does V-hat(t) change? (two decimals)
The true values are not in the span of your features. You change the state weighting d from uniform to the on-policy visit distribution. What changes?
options: Only the TD fixed point moves, never the projection itself
The value of gamma implied by the logged data
Nothing, because the projection does not depend on the weighting d
The best-fit weights, because the error at rarely visited states counts less
questions.explanation: The minimiser of the d-weighted error depends on d unless V lies in the span; changing d moves the compromise.

questions.prompt: Two-state divergence example: phi = 1 and 2, updates only at s1, gamma = 0.8, alpha = 0.25. By what factor does w grow per update? (three decimals)
A TD fixed point has value error 0.0030 and the least-squares projection of the same value function has error 0.0034, both in the same weighted norm. What do you conclude?
options: The weighting differs between the two, which is expected and harmless
The result is plausible, because TD has the lower error by design
One of the two computations is wrong, because the projection is the minimiser
questions.explanation: The projection minimises the weighted error over the span, so nothing in the span, including the TD point, can beat it.

questions.prompt: Semi-gradient TD update: w = (0, 0), phi(s) = [1, 2], r = 1, terminal transition, alpha = 0.1. What is the first weight after the update? (three decimals)
Which change removes the 'bootstrapping' vertex of the deadly triad?
options: Add a constant bias feature to the features
Use a smaller learning rate for the updates
Average the results over many more seeds
Use full Monte Carlo returns as the targets
questions.explanation: Monte Carlo targets do not use the current estimate of the next state, so they are not bootstrapped.

questions.prompt: You have 10 states and 3 features. The least-squares fit has a large error at a state the policy visits only 1% of the time. Is this evidence of a bug?
options: Not by itself: the d-weighted objective barely penalises it
No: weighted error is only defined for terminal states
Yes: tabular features should have been used with TD
Yes: the projection must be exact at every state
questions.explanation: With fewer parameters than states the fit trades off errors in proportion to d; a rare state can be poorly fit by design.
